evidence: src/middlewares/apiKeyValidator.ts: `export default async function apiKeyValidator(req, res, next)` throws `{ name: "unauthorized", message: ... }`; the status mapping is left to the error handler
src/middlewares/bodySchemaValidator.ts: `export default function bodySchemaValidator(schema: Schema)` throws `{ name: "ValidationError", message: error.details }`, the same error-object contract

src/middlewares/errorHandlerMiddleware.ts: `errorHandlerMiddleware(error: Error, ...)` is the only place that maps error names to statuses (ValidationError→422, notFound→404, alreadyExists→409, unauthorized→401, badRequest→400, dbConnection→500)

Minor: error names are raw strings with inconsistent casing and no shared type; the validators throw plain objects while the handler types its parameter as Error; the console.error/res.status().send code repeats in every branch of errorHandlerMiddleware
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The module is a cohesive set of Express request-pipeline middlewares: authentication (apiKeyValidator), request-body validation (bodySchemaValidator), and error-to-HTTP translation (errorHandlerMiddleware). The two validators follow the same contract: they throw a `{ name, message }` object or call next(). Only errorHandlerMiddleware maps error names to HTTP statuses, so that rule lives in one place and the validators don't bypass it by sending responses themselves. Weaknesses that are not failures: the error names are raw strings with inconsistent casing ("ValidationError" vs "unauthorized") and no shared type or factory; the validators throw plain objects while the handler types its parameter as Error; and the handler repeats the same console.error/res.status().send code in every branch. Separately, the handler's branches don't return, so it can try to send two responses. That is a correctness bug, outside this rule's scope. None of these splits the module's concern or duplicates the status-mapping rule across files.
